topics.title: The Promise of the Holy Spirit (Part 1) the Holy Spirit; Acts 1:3-5 - waiting for the promise.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the promises of Jesus concerning the Holy Spirit.
The students should be able to explain why the disciples waited in Jerusalem.
Introduction:
Last term we studied the life of Jesus on earth. Today we will learn about Jesus' promise to send the Holy Spirit to his disciples.
Content:
The Holy Spirit is the third person in the Trinity. Jesus promised to send the Holy Spirit to help his disciples after his ascension. In John 14:16-17, Jesus said he would ask the Father to give another Comforter. In John 16:5-16, Jesus explained that the Holy Spirit would guide them into all truth. The disciples waited in Jerusalem as Jesus commanded, just like a farmer waits for rain during the planting season.
Class activity:
Students will role-play the disciples waiting in Jerusalem, discussing what they expect when the Holy Spirit comes.
Evaluation questions:
1. Who promised to send the Holy Spirit?
2. Where did Jesus tell the disciples to wait?
3. What will the Holy Spirit do according to Jesus?
4. Why is waiting important in our Christian life?
Summary:
Jesus promised the Holy Spirit to empower his disciples, and they waited faithfully in Jerusalem as commanded.

topics.title: The Coming of the Holy Spirit reactions of the people.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe the events of Pentecost.
The students should be able to explain the significance of speaking in tongues.
Introduction:
Last week we learned about Jesus' promise to send the Holy Spirit. Today we will see how this promise was fulfilled on the Day of Pentecost.
Content:
Acts 2:1-13 tells us about the coming of the Holy Spirit. On the Day of Pentecost, the disciples were all together in one place. Suddenly, a sound like a mighty wind filled the house, and tongues of fire appeared over them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit enabled them. People from many nations heard them praising God in their own languages. Some were amazed, others wondered, and some mocked them, saying they were full of new wine.
Class activity:
Students will create a drawing showing the events of Pentecost and write one sentence explaining what happened.
Evaluation questions:
1. What happened to the disciples on the Day of Pentecost?
2. How did people react to what they saw and heard?
3. What is the significance of speaking in different languages?
4. Why is Pentecost important in Christianity?
Summary:
The Holy Spirit came upon the disciples on Pentecost, empowering them to speak in different languages and begin their ministry.

topics.title: Peter's First Speech and its Effects conversion of about 3,000 souls.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recount Peter's message on the Day of Pentecost.
The students should be able to explain the effect of Peter's speech.
Introduction:
Last week we saw how the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples. Today we will learn about Peter's first sermon and how it led to many people becoming believers.
Content:
After receiving the Holy Spirit, Peter stood up with the eleven disciples and addressed the crowd. He explained that what they were seeing was the fulfillment of Joel's prophecy. He told them that Jesus, whom they had crucified, was both Lord and Messiah. Peter called them to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus for the forgiveness of their sins. About 3,000 people believed and were baptized that day. This shows how powerful the Holy Spirit's work is, just like how a small seed can grow into a big tree.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to write a modern version of Peter's message in their own words.
Evaluation questions:
1. What was Peter's main message to the crowd?
2. How many people responded to Peter's message?
3. What does repentance mean?
4. Why was Peter able to speak boldly after receiving the Holy Spirit?
Summary:
Peter's powerful sermon, empowered by the Holy Spirit, led to the conversion of about 3,000 people on the Day of Pentecost.

topics.title: Fellowship in the Early Church (Part 1)
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list the characteristics of the early church fellowship.
The students should be able to explain the importance of unity among believers.
Introduction:
Last week we learned about the conversion of many people on the Day of Pentecost. Today we will study how these believers lived together in fellowship.
Content:
Acts 2:41-47 describes the fellowship of the early church. The believers were united in heart and mind. They shared everything they had, just like a family shares food during a Nigerian celebration. They met daily in the temple courts and broke bread in their homes. They praised God with glad and sincere hearts. The apostles performed many wonders and signs, and God added to their number daily. This fellowship was marked by love, sharing, and worship, creating a strong community that attracted others to Christianity.
Class activity:
Students will create a poster showing the key characteristics of the early church fellowship.
Evaluation questions:
1. What were the main activities of the early church fellowship?
2. How did the believers share their possessions?
3. Why was unity important in the early church?
4. What can we learn from the early church fellowship today?
Summary:
The early church showed true fellowship through sharing, worship, and unity, which helped the Christian faith grow rapidly.

topics.title: Midterm Examination
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate understanding of topics covered in Weeks 1-4.
Introduction:
This week we will have our midterm examination to assess your knowledge of the topics we have covered so far.
Content:
The examination will cover all topics from Weeks 1-4, including the Promise of the Holy Spirit, the Coming of the Holy Spirit, Peter's First Speech, and Fellowship in the Early Church. Students should review their notes and the scriptures mentioned in these lessons. The exam will test both memory and understanding of the biblical accounts and their significance in Christian life.
Class activity:
Students will complete the midterm examination paper.
Evaluation questions:
The midterm examination will consist of multiple-choice, short answer, and essay questions covering all topics from Weeks 1-4.
Summary:
The midterm examination will help you demonstrate what you have learned about the early church and the coming of the Holy Spirit.

topics.title: Fellowship in the Early Church (Part 2) 6:1-2 - Murmuring and complaints.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify challenges faced by the early church.
The students should be able to explain the story of Ananias and Sapphira.
Introduction:
Before the midterm break, we studied the fellowship of the early church. Today we will look at some challenges they faced, including the story of Ananias and Sapphira.
Content:
Acts 5:1-11 tells us about Ananias and Sapphira, who lied to the Holy Spirit. They sold their land but kept back some money for themselves, pretending to give it all to the church. Peter confronted Ananias, asking why he had let Satan fill his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit. Ananias fell down and died. Later, his wife Sapphira came in and lied too, and she also fell down and died. This shows the importance of honesty in the church. Acts 6:1-2 mentions murmuring and complaints in the church, showing that even the early church faced challenges that needed to be addressed.
Class activity:
Students will role-play a scene where they discuss how to handle problems in the church community.
Evaluation questions:
1. What did Ananias and Sapphira do wrong?
2. What happened to Ananias and Sapphira?
3. Why is honesty important in the church?
4. What challenges did the early church face according to Acts 6:1-2?
Summary:
The early church faced challenges like dishonesty and complaints, which were dealt with seriously to maintain the purity of the church.

topics.title: Midterm Break
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to rest and prepare for the second half of the term.
Introduction:
This is midterm break time. Use this period to rest and reflect on what you have learned so far.
Content:
During this break, students should take time to rest their minds and bodies. It is also a good time to review the topics covered in the first half of the term. You may read your Bible and think about how the early church's experiences can apply to your life today. Remember that even during rest, we can grow spiritually by spending quiet time in prayer and reflection.
Class activity:
Students will have a break from regular classes to rest and recharge.
Evaluation questions:
No formal evaluation during break period.
Summary:
Use this midterm break wisely to rest and prepare for the remaining lessons in the term.

topics.title: Selection of Deacons
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain why deacons were chosen in the early church.
The students should be able to list the responsibilities of deacons.
Introduction:
After the break, we return to studying the early church. Today we will learn about how the church selected deacons to help with the growing needs.
Content:
Acts 6:1-7 tells us about the selection of deacons. The early church was growing rapidly, and the Greek-speaking widows were being neglected in the daily food distribution. The apostles said it was not right for them to leave the ministry of the word to wait on tables. So they suggested choosing seven men full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom to handle this responsibility. Stephen and six others were chosen, including Philip, Procorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas. The apostles prayed and laid their hands on them. This shows how the church organized itself to meet different needs, just like a well-managed market with different sections.
Class activity:
Students will create a chart showing the qualifications and responsibilities of the first deacons.
Evaluation questions:
1. Why were deacons chosen in the early church?
2. Who were the first seven deacons mentioned?
3. What qualifications did the deacons need?
4. What role did the apostles play in selecting the deacons?
Summary:
The early church chose deacons to handle practical matters so the apostles could focus on spiritual leadership.

topics.title: Persecution of Early Believers (Part 1) 60 - Arrest and martyrdom of Stephen.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe the arrest of Peter and John.
The students should be able to explain the martyrdom of Stephen.
Introduction:
Last week we learned about the selection of deacons in the early church. Today we will begin studying the persecution faced by early believers, starting with the arrest of Peter and John and the martyrdom of Stephen.
Content:
Acts 3:1-11 and 4:1-22 tell us about the arrest of Peter and John. They healed a beggar at the Beautiful Gate and were arrested for preaching about Jesus resurrection. They were brought before the Sanhedrin but spoke boldly, saying they could not stop speaking about what they had seen and heard. Acts 6:8-15 and 7:1 describe Stephen's arrest and martyrdom. Stephen, full of faith and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. When falsely accused, he gave a powerful speech about Israel's history and Jesus. The people became angry and stoned him to death. Stephen's death marked the beginning of great persecution against the church in Jerusalem.
Class activity:
Students will write a short paragraph explaining how they would respond if faced with persecution for their faith.
Evaluation questions:
1. Why were Peter and John arrested?
2. How did Peter and John respond to their arrest?
3. What happened to Stephen?
4. Why was Stephen's death significant in the early church?
Summary:
The early church faced persecution from the beginning, with believers like Peter, John, and Stephen showing great courage in the face of opposition.

topics.title: Persecution of Early Believers (Part 2) of James.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain Saul's persecution of the church.
The students should be able to describe the martyrdom of James.
Introduction:
Last week we studied the persecution of early believers including the arrest of Peter and John and the martyrdom of Stephen. Today we will continue by learning about Saul's persecution and the martyrdom of James.
Content:
Acts 8:1-3 and 9:1-2 describe Saul's persecution of the church. Saul approved of Stephen's death and began ravaging the church, dragging off men and women and putting them in prison. He went to the high priest and asked for letters to the synagogues in Damascus so that if he found any belonging to the Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. Acts 12:1-4 tells us about the martyrdom of James, the brother of John. King Herod Agrippa I arrested James and put him to death with the sword. When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he also arrested Peter. This persecution scattered believers throughout Judea and Samaria, fulfilling Jesus' command to be his witnesses in all Judea and Samaria.
Class activity:
Students will create a timeline showing the major events of persecution during this period.
Evaluation questions:
1. Who was Saul and what did he do to the church?
2. What happened to James according to Acts 12?
3. How did the persecution affect the spread of Christianity?
4. What can we learn from the response of early believers to persecution?
Summary:
The early church faced severe persecution from figures like Saul and King Herod, but this helped spread the faith to new regions.

topics.title: Revision
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall and explain key events from the term's topics.
The students should be able to demonstrate understanding of the growth and challenges of the early church.
Introduction:
This week we will revise all the topics we have covered this term to prepare for your final examination.
Content:
We will review the Promise of the Holy Spirit, the Coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, Peter's First Speech, Fellowship in the Early Church, the selection of deacons, and the persecution faced by early believers. Students should be prepared to discuss how the Holy Spirit empowered the early church, how they maintained fellowship despite challenges, and how persecution actually helped spread Christianity. Review your notes and be ready to answer questions about key biblical passages and their significance.
Class activity:
Students will participate in a group quiz competition covering all topics from the term.
Evaluation questions:
The revision period will include practice questions covering all topics from Weeks 1-10.
Summary:
Thorough revision will help you prepare well for your final examination and better understand the growth of the early church.

topics.title: Examination
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate knowledge and understanding of all topics covered this term.
Introduction:
This week you will write your final examination for Christian Religious Studies this term.
Content:
The examination will cover all topics from Weeks 1-11, including the Promise of the Holy Spirit, the Coming of the Holy Spirit, Peter's First Speech, Fellowship in the Early Church, challenges faced by the early church, selection of deacons, and persecution of early believers. The exam will test your knowledge of biblical passages, your understanding of key events, and your ability to apply lessons from the early church to modern Christian life.
Class activity:
Students will complete the final examination paper.
Evaluation questions:
The final examination will consist of various question types covering all topics studied this term.
Summary:
The examination will assess your understanding of the growth and challenges of the early church as described in the Book of Acts.

topics.title: Closing
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to reflect on what they have learned this term.
The students should be able to identify key lessons from the study of the early church.
Introduction:
As we close this term, let's reflect on what we have learned about the early church and its growth despite challenges.
Content:
This term we have studied how the Holy Spirit empowered the early church, how believers maintained fellowship, and how they faced persecution with courage. We have seen how challenges like dishonesty and complaints were addressed, and how the church organized itself through the selection of deacons. These lessons are still relevant today for our own Christian walk and church life. As you go on holiday, remember to apply these lessons in your daily life and continue to grow in your faith.
Class activity:
Students will write one thing they have learned this term that they will apply in their life.
Evaluation questions:
No formal evaluation during closing week.
Summary:
We have completed our study of the early church this term, learning valuable lessons that can guide our Christian faith and practice today.
